translation_en: Jabir ibn Abdullah reported that the Messenger of Allah said: “Whoever gives a lifetime grant to a man and his descendants, it belongs to him and his descendants.” This wording is narrated by Yahya ibn Yahya and Muhammad ibn Rumh from al-Layth, and by Qutaybah from Layth, through Ibn Shihab, Abu Salamah, and Jabir. Yahya’s version begins: “Any man who is given a lifetime grant, it belongs to him and his descendants.”

Jabir reported that the Messenger of Allah said: “If a man gives another a lifetime grant for him and his descendants, saying, ‘I give it to you and your descendants as long as any of you remains,’ it belongs to the recipient and will not return to its owner, because it was a gift subject to inheritance.”

Jabir said that the lifetime grant approved by the Messenger of Allah was one in which the giver said, “It is yours and your descendants’.” But if he said, “It is yours for as long as you live,” it returned to the giver. Maamar said al-Zuhri gave legal rulings according to this.

Jabir reported that the Messenger of Allah ruled that a lifetime grant to a man and his descendants belonged to them outright; the giver could not impose a condition or retain a portion. Abu Salamah explained that the gift was subject to inheritance, which ended the giver’s condition.

Jabir ibn Abdullah reported that the Messenger of Allah ruled that a lifetime grant to a man and his descendants belonged to them completely, and the giver could not impose a condition or reserve a portion.
Jabir ibn Abdullah reported that the Messenger of Allah said: “A lifetime grant belongs to the person to whom it is given.”
This is another chain for the same report, from Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna through Muadh ibn Hisham, his father, Yahya ibn Abi Kathir, Abu Salamah, and Jabir.
This is another chain from Ahmad ibn Yunus through Zuhayr, Abu al-Zubayr, and Jabir, who attributed the report to the Prophet.

Jabir reported that the Messenger of Allah said: “Keep your property for yourselves and do not squander it. Whoever gives a lifetime grant, it belongs to the recipient while alive and after death, and to the recipient’s descendants.”

This report comes through other chains and has the same meaning as Abu Khaythamah’s narration. The chain includes Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah, Muhammad ibn Bishr, Hajjaj ibn Abi Uthman, Waki, Sufyan, Abd al-Warith ibn Abd al-Samad, his father and grandfather, and Ayyub, all from Abu al-Zubayr and Jabir. Ayyub’s version adds that the Ansar were giving lifetime grants to the Emigrants, and the Messenger said, “Keep your property for yourselves.”

Jabir reported a case in Madinah: a woman gave a garden as a lifetime grant to her son. He died, and later she died, leaving a child; the giver also had sons who were the recipient’s brothers. The woman’s child said the garden had returned to their family, while the giver’s sons said it had belonged to their father for life and death. They took the dispute to Tariq, freedman of Uthman. He called Jabir, who testified that the Messenger ruled a lifetime grant belonged to its recipient. Tariq ruled accordingly and wrote to Abd al-Malik, who affirmed Jabir’s testimony. The garden has remained with the recipient’s sons ever since.
Abdullah ibn Umar reported that Tariq ruled that a lifetime grant belonged to the heir, based on Jabir ibn Abdullah’s report from the Messenger of Allah.

Jabir ibn Abdullah reported that the Messenger of Allah said: “A lifetime grant is valid.” This is narrated by Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna and Muhammad ibn Bashshar through Muhammad ibn Jafar, Shubah, Qatadah, and Ata.
Jabir reported that the Prophet said: “A lifetime grant is inheritance for its recipient.” Yahya ibn Habib narrated it through Khalid ibn al-Harith, Said, Qatadah, and Ata.

Abu Hurairah reported that the Prophet said: “A lifetime grant is valid.” This chain is Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna and Ibn Bashshar, from Muhammad ibn Jafar, Shubah, Qatadah, al-Nadr ibn Anas, and Bashir ibn Nahik.
This report comes through Yahya ibn Habib and Khalid ibn al-Harith from Said and Qatadah, with the wording “inheritance for its recipient,” or perhaps “a valid grant.”

Ibn Umar reported that the Messenger of Allah said: “A Muslim who has something to bequeath should not let two nights pass without having his will written and kept with him.” The chain includes Abu Khaythamah Zuhayr ibn Harb, Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna, Yahya al-Qattan, Ubayd Allah, Nafi, and Ibn Umar.
This is the same report through Abdah ibn Sulayman and Abdullah ibn Numayr, and through Ibn Numayr from his father. They say “and he has something to bequeath,” rather than “wants to bequeath it.”

This report comes through several chains from Nafi and Ibn Umar, including Hammad ibn Zayd and Ismail ibn Ulayyah from Ayyub; Ibn Wahb from Yunus and Usamah ibn Zayd al-Laythi; and Ibn Abi Fudayk from Hisham ibn Sad. They give similar wording, saying “he has something to bequeath,” except Ayyub’s report, which says “wants to bequeath it.”

Ibn Umar reported that the Messenger of Allah said: “A Muslim who has something to bequeath should not let three nights pass without having his will written and kept with him.” Abdullah ibn Umar said that from the night he heard this, he never spent a night without having his will with him.

This is the same report through Abu al-Tahir and Harmalah from Ibn Wahb and Yunus; through Abd al-Malik ibn Shuayb, his father and grandfather, and Uqayl; and through Abd al-Razzaq and Maamar. All report it from al-Zuhri with wording like Amr ibn al-Harith’s narration.

Saad ibn Abi Waqqas said: “During the Farewell Pilgrimage, the Messenger of Allah visited me when I was gravely ill. I said, ‘Messenger of Allah, my illness is as you see, and I have wealth but only one daughter will inherit from me. Should I give two-thirds of my wealth in charity?’ He said no. I asked about half; he said no. I asked about one-third. He said, ‘One-third, and one-third is much. It is better to leave your heirs well-off than poor, begging from people. Any spending seeking Allah’s pleasure is rewarded, even the morsel you put in your wife’s mouth.’ I asked whether I would remain behind my companions. He said, ‘You will not remain and do a deed seeking Allah’s pleasure without your rank rising. Perhaps you will remain until some people benefit through you and others are harmed by you.’ He prayed that his companions’ migration be completed and that they not turn back, then said, ‘But Saad ibn Khawlah is unfortunate.’ The Messenger of Allah felt sorrow that he had died in Makkah.”

This is the same account through several chains: Qutaybah and Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah from Sufyan ibn Uyaynah; Abu al-Tahir and Harmalah from Ibn Wahb and Yunus; and Ishaq ibn Ibrahim and Abd ibn Humayd from Abd al-Razzaq and Maamar, all from al-Zuhri with a similar chain.

Saad reported that the Prophet visited him and related a similar account. This version omits the Prophet’s words about Saad ibn Khawlah, but says that he disliked dying in the land from which he had emigrated.

Saad said he was ill and asked the Prophet to let him distribute his property as he wished. The Prophet refused when he asked about half, then remained silent when he asked about one-third. Maamar said that afterward one-third was permitted.
This is the same account through Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna and Ibn Bashshar from Muhammad ibn Jafar, Shubah, and Simak. It does not include the statement that one-third was later permitted.

Saad said the Prophet visited him and he asked to bequeath all his wealth. The Prophet said no. He asked about half; the Prophet again said no. He asked about one-third, and the Prophet said: “Yes, and one-third is much.” The transmitters include al-Qasim ibn Zakariyya, Husayn ibn Ali, Zaida, Abd al-Malik ibn Umayr, and Musab ibn Saad.

Three of Saad’s children reported that the Prophet visited Saad in Makkah while he was ill and crying because he feared dying in the land from which he had emigrated, as Saad ibn Khawlah had. The Prophet prayed three times, “O Allah, heal Saad.” Saad asked whether he could bequeath all his wealth, since only his daughter would inherit. The Prophet said no to all of it, two-thirds, and half. He said one-third was allowed, but one-third was much. He added that charity from one’s wealth, spending on one’s family, and even what one’s wife eats are all charity. Leaving one’s family well-off is better than leaving them begging from people. The report is transmitted by Muhammad ibn Abi Umar through al-Thaqafi, Ayyub, Amr ibn Said, and Humayd al-Himyari from three of Saad’s children.

This is a similar account transmitted by Abu al-Rabi through Hammad and Ayyub, from Amr ibn Said and Humayd al-Himyari, who reported it from three of Saad’s children. They said Saad became ill in Makkah and the Messenger came to visit him.

This is the same account transmitted by Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna through Abd al-Ala, Hisham, Muhammad, and Humayd ibn Abd al-Rahman. Three of Saad ibn Malik’s children each related it with wording like Amr ibn Said’s report: Saad fell ill in Makkah and the Prophet came to visit him.
